content: Thalassaemia is a genetic blood disorder inherited in a recessive manner, which results in varying degrees of anaemia. In severe cases, individuals require regular blood transfusions. However, these transfusions can lead to iron overload, where excess iron accumulates in vital organs such as the heart, liver, and endocrine glands, including the pituitary gland. This iron deposition can impair the production of growth hormone, contributing to growth hormone deficiency. Growth hormone deficiency is a significant factor in the development of short stature, a common complication in individuals with thalassaemia. Growth hormone replacement therapy has been utilized in children with thalassaemia who exhibit both short stature and growth hormone deficiency. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the benefits and safety of growth hormone therapy in individuals with thalassaemia. The review was initially published in September 2017 and updated in April 2020. The search for relevant studies included the Cochrane Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register, electronic databases, handsearched journals, conference abstracts, and clinical trial registries. The most recent searches were conducted in November 2019 and January 2020. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared growth hormone therapy to placebo or standard care in individuals with any type or severity of thalassaemia. Two independent authors selected the trials, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE criteria. Only one trial met the inclusion criteria. This trial, conducted in Turkey, involved 20 children with homozygous beta thalassaemia and short stature. Ten children received daily subcutaneous growth hormone therapy at a dose of 0.7 IU/kg per week, while the other ten received standard care. The trial had a low overall risk of bias, although the selection criteria and attrition bias were unclear. The certainty of the evidence for major outcomes was moderate, primarily due to imprecision caused by the small sample size and wide confidence intervals. The trial did not assess final height or changes in height, which were pre-specified primary outcomes of the review. However, after one year, there was no significant difference between the groups in height standard deviation (SD) scores, with a mean difference (MD) of -0.09 (95% confidence interval [CI] -0.33 to 0.15). Despite this, modest improvements were observed in other outcomes for children receiving growth hormone therapy compared to the control group. These included: Change in height SD score between baseline and the final visit: MD 0.26 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.39). Height velocity: MD 2.28 cm/year (95% CI 1.76 to 2.80). Height velocity SD score: MD 3.31 (95% CI 2.43 to 4.19). Change in height velocity SD score between baseline and the final visit: MD 3.41 (95% CI 2.45 to 4.37). No adverse effects of growth hormone therapy were reported in either group. However, fasting blood glucose levels were significantly higher in the growth hormone therapy group compared to the control group, with an MD of 6.67 mg/dL (95% CI 2.66 to 10.68). Despite this, both groups' fasting glucose levels remained within the normal range. There was no significant difference between the groups in the oral glucose tolerance test at one year. The trial did not provide data beyond the one-year period. The authors concluded that the evidence from this small trial suggests that one year of growth hormone therapy may improve height velocity in children with thalassaemia. However, the height SD score in the treatment group was similar to that of the control group. There is a lack of randomized controlled trials in adults and no studies evaluating the long-term use of growth hormone therapy, its effects on final height, or its impact on quality of life. The optimal dosage and timing of growth hormone therapy remain uncertain. Larger, well-designed randomized controlled trials with longer follow-up periods are needed to address these gaps in knowledge.
